content: Deferred gratification, also known as delayed gratification, refers to the ability to resist the temptation for an immediate reward in order to obtain a more valuable reward later. This ability is often regarded as a significant personality trait that contributes to success in life. Daniel Goleman, a prominent psychologist, has emphasized that delayed gratification is a critical component of emotional intelligence. Individuals who lack this ability are often described as requiring instant gratification and may exhibit poor impulse control. Psychoanalysts have theorized that poor impulse control is associated with weak ego boundaries. This concept originates from Sigmund Freud's theory of personality, which divides the psyche into three components: the id, the ego, and the superego. The superego represents the morality principle, enforcing societal and ethical standards. The ego, functioning under the reality principle, mediates between the id's desires and the superego's moral constraints. According to this framework, individuals who struggle to delay gratification may have an overactive id that the ego and superego fail to regulate effectively. Biological factors in the brain may also contribute to poor impulse control. For instance, research has shown that children with fetal alcohol syndrome exhibit a reduced capacity to delay gratification. One of the most well-known studies on delayed gratification is the marshmallow experiment, conducted by Walter Mischel at Stanford University in the 1960s. In this experiment, four-year-old children were each given a marshmallow and told they would receive a second one if they could refrain from eating the first for 20 minutes. Some children successfully waited, while others did not. Longitudinal follow-ups revealed that the children who were able to delay gratification were better adjusted, more dependable (as reported by their parents and teachers), and scored an average of 210 points higher on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT) compared to those who could not wait. Another notable test of impulse control is the gift delay task. In this experiment, children were presented with a wrapped gift but were instructed to complete a puzzle before opening it. Researchers calculated a delay score based on how long each child resisted opening the gift. Years later, independent examiners assessed the participants and found that boys who had failed to delay gratification were described as irritable, while the girls were characterized as sulky. Conversely, boys who had successfully delayed gratification were described as attentive, and the girls were noted to be competent. Currently, a free self-report tool called the Delaying Gratification Inventory is available online as part of a research initiative by Central Michigan University. This survey evaluates individual differences in the tendency to delay gratification across six specific categories, as well as a global domain. Participants receive personalized feedback on their delayed gratification traits based on their responses.
